item.title: Tarique says Rohingya crisis can only be resolved in Myanmar
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday said a lasting solution to the Rohingya crisis lies in Myanmar, stressing that forcibly displaced Rohingyas must be able to return to their homeland voluntarily, safely, swiftly and with dignity.
“The lasting solution to the (Rohingya) crisis lies in Myanmar,” he said during a bilateral summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at the Kantei (the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office) in Tokyo.
Tarique expressed deep concerns over the deteriorating situation in Myanmar and the resulting displacement of Rohingya people, said Prime Minister's Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
He called for an end to all forms of violence, unhindered humanitarian assistance and dialogue among all parties concerned to resolve the crisis.
The prime minister appreciated Japan’s support for Bangladesh’s humanitarian efforts for Rohingyas, who were forcibly displaced from Myanmar’s Rakhine State and took shelter in Bangladesh.
He also urged Japan to remain actively engaged with all parties to help establish peace and stability in Rakhine.
During the summit, the two leaders emphasised strengthening long-standing Bangladesh-Japan relations, expanding trade and investment, and enhancing cooperation in energy security, technology, space research, infrastructure and regional and international affairs.
Tarique Rahman called for greater engagement by the Japanese government and private sector in Bangladesh’s economic development, technological advancement and industrialisation.
He also recalled the visits to Japan by his father, late president Ziaur Rahman, and the contributions of his mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, to strengthening bilateral ties, pledging to build on their legacy and take relations between the two countries to a new level.
The prime minister highlighted the two countries’ shared commitment to multilateralism, international peace and respect for international law.
He thanked Japan for supporting Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman’s election as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Tarique expressed his desire to work closely with Japan to strengthen multilateral cooperation and address global challenges during the session.
Reaffirming their shared vision of a free, open, peaceful and inclusive Indo-Pacific, he stressed greater cooperation in regional connectivity, the free flow of trade and economic growth.
Outlining Bangladesh’s ambition to become a regional hub for the economy, technology and manufacturing, the prime minister said the country can become the world’s ninth-largest consumer economy by 2030, while its gross domestic product can exceed US$1 trillion by 2034.
He said Japan holds a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh and recalled that it was among the first countries to recognise Bangladesh after its independence in 1971. Japan has since remained one of Bangladesh’s key development partners for more than five decades.
The bilateral summit between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi began at 11:45am local time at the Kantei.
The meeting followed a formal welcome at 11:30am, a guard of honour and the introduction of the two leaders’ respective delegations.
During the meeting, Tarique invited Takaichi to visit Bangladesh at a mutually convenient time, expressing hope that the long-standing friendship between the two countries will continue to deepen through mutual trust, cooperation and shared prosperity.

item.title: A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
item.description:
Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab’s plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.
“My original plan was to pursue a master’s degree,” Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria’s education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab’s plans. “Now I have to start thinking about other options,” she explained. “For example, I might have to move to another province to study.”
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.
Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.
“Even if a girl decides she won’t give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don’t want our daughters to go study somewhere else,” said Najab.
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.
“Gender doesn’t define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I’m trying to meet,” Najab argued. “In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let’s see where the best people are, regardless of gender.”
Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. “A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying,” she told DW. “We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let’s be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.
The sectors from which women have been excluded “require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites,” said al-Yaser. “These conditions suit young men more than women.”
A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.
Does this mean Syria’s new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women’s rights?
Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. “The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria’s international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women’s role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes,” the organization said.
Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.
All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government’s alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.
The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.
Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn’t an uncommon attitude in the Middle East’s more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.
In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was “in a limited and largely symbolic capacity,” the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn’t make it right, human rights advocates have said.
“Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it,” Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. “Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society’s perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles.”
The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women’s Political Movement.
“When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them,” al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it’s still unclear as to whether “gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria.”
But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. “Will Syria’s new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed,” she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. “Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?”

item.title: Zahed: BNP won’t back extrajudicial killings
item.description:
The BNP fought against enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings over the past 17 years and will not backtrack on that position after forming the government, Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said on Tuesday, adding that the prime minister will take the final decision about the inspector general of police over his crossfire remarks.
“If a state or government kills someone extrajudicially, it ceases to function as a state and behaves like a thug,” Zahed said while speaking at a press briefing on the progress of various government activities at the Secretariat.
No democratic government can support extrajudicial killings, he said, stressing that the state must arrest criminals and hand them over to the judicial system for trial.
“Anyone can commit murder. A state becomes a state when it exercises the authority to deliver justice,” he added.
A death sentence can be imposed through judicial proceedings, but extrajudicial killing can never be an act of the state, the adviser said, adding that the state can arrest an accused person and hand them over to the judiciary, exercising the executive authority and laws can be amended, if necessary, but there can be no scope for extrajudicial killings.
He said the government has no intention of remaining in power after its five-year term through night-time voting or dummy elections. “It will, therefore, avoid any action that can damage its credibility, as incidents such as extrajudicial killings will undermine public confidence in the government.”
Asked about IGP Md Ali Hossain Fakir’s remarks that crossfire operations could be carried out if the government gives permission, Zahed said he believed the police chief retreated from his earlier position in subsequent remarks. “He also stepped back from serious allegations he made about journalists in general,” he said, adding that he thought the issue should now be put to rest.
Asked whether the IGP should be allowed to remain in office even after clarifying his remarks, he said the matter is for journalists to assess.
The adviser said he felt the situation would have been problematic had the police chief continued to stand by his earlier statement.
He also stressed that government officials are not obliged to carry out illegal orders and public servants must perform their duties in accordance with the law.
Zahed also said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will take the final decision about the IGP after returning from the Japan visit.
Responding to a question about the arrest of a woman entrepreneur in Bhaluka, Mymensingh, for regretting voting for the BNP on Facebook live, he said he did not consider the position taken by local BNP activists who protested against her remarks to be justified.
Police took the woman into custody following the protests and later sent her to court under Section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Zahed said people have the right to express such views. “Many people in Bangladesh, including some who make offensive remarks about the Prime Minister, are expressing their opinions without facing similar action,” he said, adding that such remarks can certainly be made.
He, however, said the matter is now within the jurisdiction of the judiciary, expressing hope that investigators will not treat the woman’s remarks as a criminal offence.
Asked about the reported vandalism and looting of the homes of three Hindu families in Pirganj, Rangpur, the adviser said he heard that police were deployed and action was taken in this regard.
He said there was a tendency among some extremist groups in Bangladesh to act aggressively. “Such tendencies increased during the interim government’s tenure, and appropriate action was not taken against such incidents in many cases,” he added.
Zahed also assured that the current government will take action against such crimes. “You cannot expect to remain beyond the reach of justice under this government. I assure you of that,” he said.
Members of the Hindu community also want to live safely in a liberal democratic country, he said, adding that people have expectations from political parties entrusted with governing the country, and the BNP will have to fulfil those expectations.

item.title: HC gives task force six more months to probe Sagar-Runi murder
item.description:
The High Court has granted a task force investigating the murders of journalist couple Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi another six months to complete its probe.
The court also summoned the task force chief and Tanvir Zoha, an information technology expert and prosecutor at the International Crimes Tribunal, to provide an update on the investigation on April 27 next year. They have been directed to appear with relevant documents, and the court will hear their statements in camera.
A High Court bench comprising Justice Shikder Md Mahmudur Razi and Justice Fatema Anwar passed the order on Tuesday.
Senior lawyers Monzil Morshed and Shishir Manir appeared for the couple's family, while Attorney General Ruhul Quddus Kazal represented the state.
On September 30, 2024, the High Court ordered the removal of the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) from the investigation and directed the formation of a high-level task force under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The court set April 6, 2025, as the deadline for submitting the investigation report.
The ministry subsequently formed the task force. However, the investigation did not progress as scheduled, as the High Court was on vacation on the designated date. The state later sought additional time, and the case was placed on the High Court's hearing list again.
Sagar, news editor of Maasranga Television, and Runi, a senior reporter at ATN Bangla, were murdered at their rented apartment in the capital's West Rajabazar area on the night of February 11, 2012. Their only son, Mahir Sarowar Megh, was at home at the time.
Runi's brother, Nausher Ali Roman, filed a murder case with Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station. Local police initially investigated the case before it was transferred to the Detective Branch three days later.
After the Detective Branch failed to make progress, the case was handed over to RAB on April 18, 2012.

item.title: Power outage hits Secretariat, key areas of Dhaka
item.description:
A fault in the Meghnaghat-Haripur national grid line disrupted electricity supply to the Secretariat, several areas of Dhaka and parts of Chittagong on Tuesday.
The outage occurred at 12:43pm, leaving several areas of the capital without electricity.
Power Grid Bangladesh said the disruption affected areas including Bhulta, Haripur, Siddhirganj, Gulshan, Rampura, Ullon and Motijheel. Parts of Chittagong also experienced power cuts.
An official responsible for electricity at the Public Works Ministry in the Secretariat said the Dhaka Power Distribution Company Limited (DPDC) had informed him that the outage was caused by a grid failure.
Power Grid Bangladesh said the technical cause of the outage was yet to be determined. Restoration work was underway, with engineers reconnecting affected areas in phases. The national grid system is under the supervision of the National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC).
In an emergency press release, the Power Division said efforts were underway to restore electricity supply. Power was gradually returning to affected areas, with full restoration expected shortly.
Power Grid Bangladesh later announced that restoration of the national grid had been completed at 2:30pm, with all grid lines and substations operational.
The agency said electricity supply remained normal in the northern parts of the country and other unaffected areas.
Several areas of the capital, including the Secretariat and its surroundings, Moghbazar, Modhubagh, Shantinagar, Malibagh and Khilgaon, were reported to be without electricity.
In an emergency press release issued on Tuesday, the Power Division said a technical fault had disrupted electricity supply to parts of Dhaka and Chitttagong, adding that urgent efforts were underway to restore power.
Power plants were being brought back online in phases, and scattered load-shedding was expected to ease as electricity generation increased, the agency said.
It apologised for the temporary inconvenience caused by the unexpected power disruption.

item.title: UCB, Mastercard and GP unveils co-branded sticker payment card
item.description:
United Commercial Bank PLC (UCB), Mastercard and Grameenphone on Tuesday unveiled a co-branded sticker payment card, offering consumers in Bangladesh a simple and convenient way to make contactless payments while enjoying cashback, rewards and exclusive lifestyle benefits.
The event was attended by Brent T Christensen, US Ambassador to Bangladesh, as chief guest.
Also present were Sharif Zahir, chairman, UCB; Mohammad Mamdudur Rashid, chief executive officer, UCB; Gautam Aggarwal, division president, India & South Asia, Mastercard; Sandun Hapugoda, country manager, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bangladesh, Bhutan & Nepal, Mastercard; Zakia Sultana, country manager, Bangladesh, Mastercard; Solaiman Alam, chief product officer, Grameenphone, along with senior executives from the three organizations.
The prepaid sticker card can be attached to a smartphone or another suitable item, allowing cardholders to make payments by simply tapping it on a contactless-enabled point-of-sale (POS) terminal.
This eliminates the need to carry a conventional payment card, making everyday transactions quicker and easier.
The card combines UCB’s banking services, Mastercard’s secure payment technology and Grameenphone’s MyGP digital ecosystem, enabling cardholders to enjoy seamless payments alongside a range of other benefits.

Through this collaboration, we are introducing an innovative form factor that expands consumer choice while supporting the continued growth of contactless payments in Bangladesh.”
The card comes with a first-year fee waiver, while the annual fee will be waived for cardholders spending Tk100,000 or more in a calendar year.
Solaiman Alam, chief product officer, Grameenphone, said: “As consumers increasingly embrace digital lifestyles, they are looking for payment solutions that are simple, convenient and relevant to their everyday needs. This association reflects our commitment to creating greater value for people through digital innovation.”
The introduction of co-branded sticker payment card reflects the shared commitment of UCB, Mastercard and Grameenphone to accelerating the adoption of contactless payments and making digital transactions more secure and rewarding for consumers across Bangladesh.

item.title: Sajek residents demand probe into attack on blockade
item.description:
Sajek residents and local organizations have demanded punishment for those responsible for an alleged attack on a peaceful road blockade on October 22, compensation for affected traders and withdrawal of a case against protesters.
In a memorandum submitted to the government on Monday, the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee and Sajek Karbari Association also demanded an impartial judicial inquiry into the incident and the removal of armed members of the Santu Larma-led faction of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (PCJSS) from the area, said a press release.
The signatories alleged that the armed group had been threatening residents, firing indiscriminately and extorting money from Jhum cultivators, creating fear and insecurity in several villages.
According to the statement, the group began armed activities in the area on August 31. Its members allegedly demanded Tk1,000 for every ari of Jhum land and extorted money from owners of rice-processing machines, turmeric-grinding machines and engine-powered boats. A nine-year-old girl, Kosmita Tripura, was reportedly injured by gunfire.
Residents said they had repeatedly urged the local military administration to take action against the group but received no effective response. They began an indefinite road blockade on October 11, temporarily suspending it after the army sought additional time. The blockade resumed on October 15, was suspended for Durga Puja and restarted on October 22.
The signatories alleged that security personnel attacked protesters with batons without provocation while discussions were underway about allowing stranded tourists to pass. Army personnel subsequently opened fire, vandalised and looted shops and homes in Ujopazar, and injured several people, they claimed.
They also alleged that army and police personnel later attempted to arrest SSC examinee Jharna Chakma over her participation in the blockade.
The memorandum was signed by Babudhan Chakma, convener of the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee; Natun Joy Chakma, president of the Sajek Karbari Association; Ushatan Chakma of the Student-People's Struggle Council; Jiko Chakma of the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee; and Sadhana Debi Chakma of Sajek Women's Society.

item.title: Man beaten to death over alleged mugging in Jatrabari, another injured
item.description:
A 32-year-old man was beaten to death and another injured by a mob over alleged mugging at Bibir Bagicha on Demra Road in Dhaka’s Jatrabari area on Tuesday morning.
The deceased was identified as Joni, 32, son of the late Abul Kashem, from Matbor Goli in the Kazlarpar area of Jatrabari.
The injured, Nisat Miah, 27, son of Mohsin Miah from the Kalapatti area of Jatrabari, is currently undergoing treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) under police custody.
According to police, the incident took place between 7am and 8am near Gate No-4 of Bibir Bagicha on Demra Road under Jatrabari Police Station.
Jatrabari Police Station Sub-Inspector (SI) Md Hasan said a group of youths was allegedly committing muggings in the area in the morning when local residents chased them.
While others managed to flee, locals caught Joni and Nisat and beat them up, leaving Joni dead on the spot.
Upon receiving information, police recovered Joni's body from the scene and sent it to the DMCH morgue for an autopsy after completing legal formalities.
Police said legal proceedings regarding the incident are underway.

item.title: Coco peat trial explores soil-free farming in Gazipur
item.description:
No ploughing, no soil beds and no conventional land preparation. Instead, rows of polybags filled with coco peat, a growing medium made from coconut husks, are nurturing cucumber plants in Sapmara village of Gazipur. As the plants grow, so does farmer Ferdous Mia's hope that crops can be cultivated successfully without soil.
Ferdous is not pursuing a large commercial venture. His initiative is a small-scale experiment to assess the feasibility of soil-free farming under local conditions, including its production potential, ease of cultivation and overall costs.
The experiment is underway on three kathas of land in Sapmara village in Pubail, Gazipur city. Known locally for his enthusiasm for farming, Ferdous has long cultivated papaya and various traditional vegetables. He has now turned to soilless cultivation in search of an alternative approach to farming.
He is receiving guidance from Ariful Islam, a Bangladeshi expatriate farmer who gained experience in coco peat-based cultivation in Malaysia. Together, they are exploring how the technique can be adapted to local conditions.
In the first phase, Ferdous has installed 200 polybags filled with coco peat instead of soil. Made from processed coconut husks and fibres, the material provides a growing medium that retains moisture, allows air to reach plant roots and supports nutrient management. Cucumber plants are now growing in the bags.
"I am interested in adopting new and modern technologies alongside conventional farming. That is why I have started soil-free cultivation using coco peat. Although the initial cost is somewhat higher, I hope the expenses will come down if production becomes regular," Ferdous said.
Soilless cultivation is not new to global agriculture. Techniques such as hydroponics and coco peat-based growing systems are used in various countries, particularly where farmland is limited and growers seek to make more efficient use of available space.
For Ferdous, however, the immediate challenge is to determine whether the method can deliver practical and economic benefits in Bangladesh. He is monitoring the plants' growth, water requirements, nutrient needs and susceptibility to pests and diseases. The decisive test will be the yield and whether it justifies the investment.
If the experiment proves successful, he plans to extend the method to other fruits and vegetables. He believes soil-free cultivation could help increase production in limited spaces at a time when agricultural land is shrinking and farmers face seasonal challenges.
"Technology is playing an increasingly important role in agriculture. If the experiment succeeds, we can try to produce more in a smaller space. I plan to work with other crops as well," he said.
With pressure on agricultural land mounting and food demand remaining high, finding ways to increase production within limited spaces has become increasingly important. Yet growing crops in coco peat does not automatically guarantee higher yields or greater profits.
The method's viability will depend on several factors, including initial investment, the cost of coco peat and other inputs, labour requirements, nutrient management and the quantity and quality of the harvest. Ferdous's experiment could offer a small but useful insight into how the technique performs under local conditions.
Farmers in Sapmara are also watching the cucumber plants grow in the coco peat-filled bags, and the initiative has sparked curiosity about the alternative technique. If the trial succeeds, it could encourage others in the area to explore technology-based cultivation.
Kaliganj Upazila Agriculture Officer Hasibul Hasan said seedlings produced using coco peat were of good quality and less susceptible to diseases.
He described coco peat-based cultivation as a potential tool for improving farmers' livelihoods, adding that proper crop management and the use of improved technology could help increase their financial returns.

item.title: Article 9 Committee launched to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities
item.description:
A new advocacy platform, the Article 9 Committee, has been launched to promote the implementation of Article 9 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), which requires measures to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities across all areas of life.
The committee held its inaugural meeting at the Omni Residency Hotel in Baridhara, Dhaka, on Monday, with a focus on addressing barriers in infrastructure, transport, information and communication technology, and public services.
The meeting was organized by the women-led Bangladesh Society for the Change and Advocacy Nexus (B-SCAN), with support from the Centre for Services and Information on Disability (CSID) and the Centre for Disabilities in Development (CDD), under the Disability Inclusive Civic Engagement (DiCE) project. The project is supported by the Nagorikata – Civic Engagement Fund, managed by GFA.
Article 9 of the UNCRPD calls on states to ensure that persons with disabilities can access the physical environment, transportation, information and communications, and other facilities and services open or provided to the public on an equal basis with others. Accessibility is essential to independent living and full participation in society.
Representatives attend the inaugural meeting of the Article 9 Committee, formed to promote accessibility for persons with disabilities, in Baridhara, Dhaka, on Monday, October 26, 2026. Photo: Courtesy
The committee aims to raise awareness of accessibility rights, bring together organisations of persons with disabilities, civil society groups, development organisations, professional bodies and academic institutions, and strengthen coordination and accountability in implementing accessibility standards.
Accessibility extends beyond ramps to include accessible buildings and toilets, public transport, websites, sign language and information in accessible formats. Universal design can also benefit older people, children, pregnant women and those with temporary mobility difficulties.
B-SCAN Executive Director Salma Mahbub said the platform would work nationally to make Bangladesh accessible to all by combining the knowledge and experience of civil society organisations.
The committee's initial priorities include identifying barriers across infrastructure, transport, communication technologies and services; engaging responsible institutions; and advocating for universal design to make accessibility an integral part of planning and service delivery.
Representatives from B-SCAN, CDD and CSID attended the meeting, alongside those from WaterAid, Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon (BAPA), the Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP), Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST), BRAC, Friendship, SERAC, WBB Trust, the Women with Disabilities Development Foundation (WDDF), SMF, the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI), and Mass Studio.

item.title: Persons with disabilities demand immediate anti-discrimination law
item.description:
Persons with disabilities and rights advocates have urged the government to immediately enact a comprehensive anti-discrimination law to ensure inclusion, protection and equal rights for all marginalized communities.
The call came at a consultation organized jointly by the Centre for Disabilities in Development (CDD) and Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) at the Shakti Foundation Training and Research Center in Akran, Savar, on Tuesday.
Held under the Disability Inclusive Civic Engagement (DiCE) project, the consultation brought together persons with disabilities, civil society representatives and government officials to review the draft Anti-Discrimination Bill and propose recommendations from a disability rights perspective.
The project is funded by Switzerland, Canada and the European Union, implemented through GFA Consulting Group GmbH and supported by the Nagorikata – Civic Engagement Fund.
Wasiur Rahman Tonmoy, lead – Youth & Social Cohesion at MJF, presented the keynote paper, outlining discrimination faced by marginalized groups in education, healthcare, employment and public and private services. These groups include Dalits, Indigenous people in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, tea garden workers and persons with disabilities.
KM Shahiduzzaman, upazila social services officer in Savar, attended as chief guest and stressed the need for enforceable legal protections and coordination between government agencies and non-governmental organisations to improve access to essential services.
Advocate Ruma Sultana, programme coordinator at MJF, highlighted the need for continued consultations with diverse communities to refine the proposed legislation. She was involved in drafting the initial Anti-Discrimination Bill, 2022.
Umme Farhana Zarif Kanta, deputy director and team lead for PROKAS at Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST), called for stronger partnerships with grassroots organizations to ensure persons with disabilities are represented in legislative advocacy.
The consultation included 48 persons with disabilities: 25 with visual impairments, 14 with physical disabilities, seven with hearing impairments and two with cerebral palsy. Sign language interpretation was provided by Iftekhar Ahmed Shorful.
Facilitated by Tonmoy, participants worked in five groups to review the draft bill and develop recommendations.
They called for the legislation to be enacted under the title “Anti-Discrimination Law” and for its definitions of discrimination to be aligned with existing national laws and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD).
Other recommendations included incorporating relevant provisions of the Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act 2013 into the proposed law, ensuring representation of persons with disabilities on monitoring committees and the proposed National Anti-Discrimination Commission, and simplifying complaint procedures and access to legal aid.
Participants also called for effective enforcement and accountability mechanisms covering both public and private sectors.
Anika Rahman Lipy, assistant director of training at CDD, delivered the closing remarks and vote of thanks. Participants pledged to continue engaging with policymakers to advance the proposed law.

item.title: Man jailed for embezzling Tk6 crore in Rajuk plot scam
item.description:
A Dhaka court has sent Munshi Manzur-e-Elahi, also known as Manjurul Alam, to jail after rejecting his bail petition in a case over the alleged embezzlement of Tk6.23 crore from a businessman by promising to arrange a five-katha Rajuk plot in Uttara.
Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Md Zakir Hossain passed the order on Tuesday. Abdulllah Al Mamun, a lawyer for the complainant, confirmed the matter.
According to the case statement, the complainant, Md Nasir, proprietor of Prashanti Enterprise, knew the accused and had been involved in a joint land trading business with them in Dhaka.
Under an oral agreement, Nasir was entitled to 50% of the profits from land sales, with the remaining half going to the accused.
The accused allegedly told Nasir that a five-katha Rajuk plot was available in Uttara for Tk5–6 crore and could later be sold for Tk9–10 crore. Persuaded by the offer, Nasir visited the plot on August 1, 2023, and agreed to invest.
The complaint alleges that the accused subsequently collected Tk6.23 crore from Nasir in instalments through pay orders and cash, claiming the money was needed for the advance payment and registration of the land.
Several crore taka were transferred through pay orders issued by City Bank and IFIC Bank in favour of Md Robiul Alam, proprietor of Rafin Enterprise, and another accused, Munshi Manzur-e-Elahi.
Other alleged members of the group, including Rafiqul Islam, Md Anisur Rahman Mia Hasib, Hasna Hena and Asif Hasan Tulip, also collected cash from Nasir at different times, according to the complaint.
Despite receiving the money, the accused allegedly delayed handing over the plot. They later stopped answering Nasir's calls and vacated their office in Sector 16 of Uttara after locking it, the complaint says.
When Nasir sought a refund on December 1, 2024, the accused allegedly refused to return the money.
Nasir filed a Complaint Register (CR) case with the court on December 29, 2024. The court took cognisance of the case the same day and directed the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) to investigate. Following the investigation, the CID submitted its report on June 30 this year.
Meanwhile, victims formed a human chain on the court premises from Tuesday morning until afternoon, demanding Manjurul Alam's trial.
They also called for the swift arrest of other alleged members of the fraud syndicate, the recovery of the money and stronger intervention by the authorities.

item.title: No envy, no secrets: How Spain's Gipuzkoa became football coaching hotbed
item.description:
Premier League heavyweights Liverpool, Arsenal and Chelsea clash this week with an unlikely thread linking them -- the men in charge all hail from the small Basque province of Gipuzkoa.
Andoni Iraola's Liverpool host Xabi Alonso's Chelsea in the League Cup on Wednesday, and then Mikel Arteta's English champions Arsenal on Sunday 1 in the Premier League
Unai Emery, a fourth Premier League coach from Gipuzkoa, takes Aston Villa to face giants Barcelona on November 3 in the Champions League.
So how did Spain's smallest province, of just 1,980 square kilometres (765 square miles), with a population of around 730,000, produce 20 percent of the Premier League's coaches?
A good starting point is one man, who mentored them all but, unlike Alonso or Arteta, is little known outside of the region -- 80-year-old Mikel Etxarri.
"A wise man and a master of football, the teacher of teachers," Josu Zubia Ramos, the Gipuzkoa football federation's director of coaching, told AFP.
Etxarri, whom the federation's coaching school is named after, has worked tirelessly for over half a century to spread his ideas.
"We Basque coaches have been fortunate to have a very strong bond between us," Etxarri told AFP, days after he was honoured for his career at a friendly between Real Sociedad and Athletic Bilbao in October.
"I think we've been lucky enough to live professional football without being professionals in that sense, without showing that passion for money, but rather a passion for knowledge."
Once, when asked about why coaches from the region were so successful, Arteta highlighted the "passion" of his people and "the education we all got".
An education which began as kids. Arteta, Iraola and Alonso all played in the same midfield aged eight -- for youth football club Antiguoko Kirol Elkartea, in San Sebastian.
Their shirts hang in the club offices, with the coaches never forgetting their roots.
Current Arsenal midfielder Martin Zubimendi is another Antiguoko graduate.
Overcoming limited resources Historically, Real Sociedad and Athletic Bilbao have provided Basque football's core.
Athletic, based in neighbouring Bizkaia, still operates its famous local player policy, while Real Sociedad abandoned its own restrictions on signing players from outside the region in 1989, but their academy remains an important source.
The pathway from academy to first team seems clearer than at other clubs, with players focused on how to compete for their local team, and give back afterwards.
Their fans expect success despite their limited resources compared to giants Real Madrid and Barcelona. Some of that gap is made up for in work rate and competitive spirit.
Both teams have in recent years won the Copa del Rey and competed in the Champions League.
Good coaching produces better players, players who understand the game deeply can become coaches themselves, and those coaches pass on their ideas -- a 'virtuous cycle'.
"There's no envy -- I don't see envy in the way people move -- what I see is that people want to perform, they want knowledge, they want information. And that's the space we all operate in," continued Etxarri.
Another recurring theme is a culture of high standards and self-improvement.
"I think we have a very strong, very high idea of performance, of demands, and of hard work, right? That's because in any field, not just football, the Basque coach is demanding of himself," added Etxarri.
"Take my own case as an example -- I've gone more than 60 years in a row without missing a single year."
Etxarri signed Alonso from Antiguoko in 1999 as Real Sociedad sporting director, and he also coached Eibar and the Basque national team.
The region has its own language, Euskara, and it's not just football where Gipuzkoans excel -- San Sebastian boasts the world's highest concentration of Michelin-starred restaurants per capita.
In the wet and cloudy Basque country, there is a strong outdoor sporting tradition. In Gipuzkoa, youngsters under 10 undertake multiple disciplines, rather than specialising in one.
Local sports such as stone-lifting and wood-cutting remain part of the culture.
"(Success is) tied a bit to the local culture, to Basque culture, Gipuzkoan culture, to how our society is, to teamwork, to how club culture has been lived over the years, to how we identify with a project when we get involved and wear a badge on our chest," explained Zubia Ramos.
"We throw ourselves into it as if we had started our careers there or had been born there.
"England has quite a lot in common with us -- a bit in terms of climate -- but above all in terms of the philosophy of how football is lived there, which is similar to Gipuzkoa."
500 coaches Many coaches gain licences in Gipuzkoa. Will the province continue to provide?
"Look, right now our coaching school is going through a really good spell," Zubia Ramos said.
"We have more enrolments than ever. For such a small population... this season we have more than 500 coaches enrolled in our school.
"What does that mean? It means there's a real interest in education, in self-improvement... I see how excited our coaches are about working."
The numbers suggest the pipeline is unlikely to dry up, with the next Arteta, Alonso or Iraola likely sitting in one of those classrooms right now.

item.title: Nadal returns for Vegas hardcourt event Los Angeles
item.description:
Rafael Nadal will return to hardcourt competition for the first time since his retirement in November 2024 in a one-night Las Vegas exhibition event next February, organizers announced on Monday.
The 40-year-old Spanish left-hander who won 22 Grand Slam singles titles will compete in "The MGM Slam" on February 28, 2027, at T-Mobile Arena.
Other players and a format for the event will be disclosed later.
Nadal, winner of a record 14 French Open singles titles, makes a hardcourt return in Vegas after playing in an exhibition event at his academy in Spain earlier this month.

item.title: Surrey coach Batty quits to join IPL side Chennai
item.description:
Gareth Batty has stepped down as the head coach of English county Surrey to become an assistant to Zaheer Khan at Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings.
Batty was among the names touted as a possible contender for the England test job after Brendon McCullum was sacked. But the 49-year-old former Surrey and England offspinner lost out to Stephen Fleming, who left CSK after 18 seasons in July ahead of taking over as England test coach.

item.title: An opportunity to build industrial capacity
item.description:
Bangladesh’s medical device market represents a significant economic opportunity that still remains largely untapped. As demand for healthcare grows, the country continues to depend heavily on imported equipment and supplies, leaving a potentially valuable domestic industry underdeveloped.
This needs to change -- not only to reduce import dependence, but also to strengthen our healthcare system and create new avenues for investment and employment.
While developing a domestic medical device industry will require considerable investment, technical expertise, quality control, and strict adherence to international standards, these challenges should encourage us to develop the necessary capacity rather than remain content with importing products that could eventually be manufactured at home.
The first step must, therefore, be creating a supportive environment for local manufacturers. Access to affordable financing, tax incentives for genuine investment, reliable infrastructure, and streamlined regulatory procedures can encourage businesses to enter the sector. Partnerships between local entrepreneurs, universities, research institutions, and international manufacturers can also facilitate technology transfer and help develop a skilled workforce.
Quality must remain central to this effort: Medical devices directly affect patient safety, and domestic production cannot be allowed to become an excuse to compromise with our standards.
Strong regulatory oversight, transparent certification procedures and investment in research and development will be essential to building confidence among healthcare providers and patients.
Additionally, where locally manufactured products meet the necessary quality and performance requirements, government hospitals could be encouraged to consider them, giving domestic businesses a dependable market in which to grow.
Such support, however, must promote genuine competitiveness rather than protect inefficient producers indefinitely.
Ultimately, our growing healthcare needs should be seen as an opportunity to build industrial capacity. Reducing import dependence will certainly take time, sustained investment, and consistent policies, but with the right support, Bangladesh can turn an overlooked market into a source of economic growth, skilled employment, and greater healthcare security.
