item.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil refinery, blasts shake Riyadh
item.description:
Yemen’s Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil refinery with a ballistic missile on Tuesday, as blasts shook the capital of the world’s top crude exporter.
Saudi Arabia, the Middle East’s largest economy, has suffered weeks of strikes from the Iran-backed Houthis against oil and civilian sites including Riyadh’s international airport.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, saying the strike caused “massive fires.”
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis earlier said it had shot down three missiles fired by the group towards the Eastern Province.
A resident in the city of Al Khobar, south of the Ras Tanura complex, told AFP he heard explosions around dawn and received a text message alert.
“We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang,” the resident said.
Maritime security agency Vanguard said a fire was reported in the Ras Tanura area in the early hours of Tuesday after an attack.
“The fire has reportedly been contained, while the extent of damage and any impact on oil-loading operations remain unclear at current,” Vanguard said.
The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia’s Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and a cornerstone of the kingdom’s energy sector.
The complex has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by strikes blamed on Iran, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.
Meanwhile a series of explosions echoed across the capital, Riyadh, shaking office windows in the city center. A text message alert warned residents to seek shelter.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted two ballistic missiles that were fired at Riyadh.
Earlier, a Houthi official said the Egyptian parliament’s decision to authorize defensive military support for Saudi Arabia amounted to a declaration of war.
Egypt’s parliament authorized the measure on Monday, following a request from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
“It is truly remarkable that while these people go to discuss what they call ‘peace in the region,’ Egypt and its parliament declare support for the so-called defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, declare war against the Republic of Yemen,” said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, in a Telegram post.
It was not clear exactly what support was on offer from Egypt, which has the Arab world’s largest military.
Al-Houthi’s statement also pointed to Monday’s visit to Tehran by the Saudi defense minister, Pakistan’s army chief and Turkiye’s intelligence chief, in a bid to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East war.
Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad recently signed a Nato-style defense pact in Mecca, pledging to consider an attack on one country as an attack on all three.
Turkiye and Pakistan have not announced any strikes on the Houthis during the group’s weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Al-Houthi said the group was “not afraid of any alliance that may be formed.”
Yemen’s largely dormant conflict reignited in July, further destabilizing the region months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing swathes of Red Sea coastline in a major offensive in September.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.
This month the Houthis ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, forcing the cancellation of flagship events and shutting down Riyadh’s airport for two weeks.
The Houthis’ war with the Saudi-led coalition began in 2015, months after they ousted the internationally recognized government from the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

item.title: India media groups challenge new data privacy rules in top court
item.description:
India’s Supreme Court on Tuesday sought the government’s response to a challenge by news publishers who say changes to data privacy rules threaten press freedom.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government introduced the rules last year to guide the law to strengthen personal data protection, but critics say their sweeping scope risks undermining public interest reporting.
The new rules “fail to provide any exemption in favor of journalistic activity” and “threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity,” according to the petition by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents some of India’s biggest news organizations.
They include Network18, part of the Reliance conglomerate led by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, and NDTV, owned by the Adani Group, founded by Gautam Adani -- two tycoons who are both close to Modi.
“We think it could have an impact on investigative journalism and compromise sources,” Sujata Gupta of the DNPA told AFP.
Data privacy laws in several parts of the world, including the European Union, provide specific exemptions for journalism.
The law’s requirement to disclose all personal data processed, without a public interest exemption, would “seriously hinder investigative reporting and could discourage whistleblowers from coming forward,” international media watchdog Reporters Without Borders said in a statement.
Independent activists and smaller news organizations have also challenged provisions removing exemptions for personal information sought under India’s Right To Information (RTI) transparency law.
“The removal of the public interest override... of the RTI Act now allows information offices of the government to withhold information that is deemed ‘personal’ even if it has significant connection to a public activity or public interest,” argues a legal challenge filed by investigative news website, The Reporters’ Collective.
Critics have long accused Modi’s Hindu nationalist government of undermining press freedom, a charge it denies. The court will next hear the matter on November 17.

item.title: Norway, Finland leaders hold ‘frank and substantive’ talk with Putin
item.description:
Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister held a “frank and substantive” discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday about efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Nordic leaders said.
“The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The statement noted that the call had been “held in consultation with Ukraine” and followed a meeting in Oslo on October 20 between Store, Stubb and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as US envoy Steve Witkoff.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the meeting remotely.
After the Oslo talks, Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg to meet Putin.
Stubb and Store initiated Tuesday’s call to discuss “efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe,” their statement said.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation,” Store said.
Stubb described the discussion between the three as “frank and substantive.”
Shortly after the announcement of the call, Kyiv said Zelensky had spoken to the Nordic leaders about the conversation with Putin.
Stubb confirmed the talks with Zelensky in a social media post and commented: “Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace.”
The leaders stressed that they were representing their own countries and had not spoken on behalf of Europe, but Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen bemoaned that they had gone “solo.”
“I’m very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn’t been coordinated with any of the rest of us,” she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders, including Store and Stubb, in Finland.
“I honestly don’t know what those two countries think they can achieve with this,” she said.
Relations between Ukraine and the United States have become strained again after Trump this month suddenly announced a deal with Russia for diesel, as part of his efforts to lower oil prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Ukraine reacted with dismay after Trump also waived sanctions against Russia and appeared to again pivot to Putin.
The Oslo meeting followed furious diplomatic efforts in Washington, Kyiv and Western capitals to calm the situation.
Norway and Finland, both Nato members, share borders with Russia and the statement emphasised that the countries are “firm supporters of Ukraine.”

item.title: Rizvi: IGP’s crossfire remarks have put govt in an awkward position
item.description:
BNP acting secretary general Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Tuesday said the Inspector General of Police’s (IGP) remarks about reinstating crossfire have caused unease within the government.
“We feel deeply saddened that the head of the police force, who is part of the government, would talk about crossfire. If it was a slip of the tongue, that would be a different matter. But such remarks put the government in an awkward position,” he said.
Rizvi made the remarks while inaugurating a free medical camp in front of the BNP’s central office at Naya Paltan, Dhaka, marking the 48th founding anniversary of Jatiotabadi Jubo Dal.
Rizvi said there are adequate laws to combat terrorism and crime, and law enforcement agencies are responsible for enforcing those.
He said the country endured 17 years of what he described as inhumane misrule involving crossfire killings, enforced disappearances, secret killings and bloodshed.
After years of struggle against such practices, the country experienced the July uprising and August 5, followed by the BNP coming to power through a free and fair electoral process, he said.
Rizvi said people across the country expect a humane Bangladesh under Tarique Rahman’s leadership, adding that such remarks from the head of a law enforcement agency are deeply concerning.
Rizvi said Tarique Rahman’s commitment to building a humane Bangladesh was reflected in initiatives such as the Family Card and Farmers’ Card, and canal excavation programs.
He said these initiatives are aimed at making Bangladesh a more liveable country, describing this as a central part of Tarique Rahman’s vision and development plan.
Referring to concerns about rising juvenile delinquency and crime in several areas of Dhaka, he said he believes the police force has many honest and capable officers who can effectively tackle crime if allowed to work.
“If the law is properly enforced without any influence, crime can be eliminated from society,” he said.
Rizvi said extrajudicial methods could never be an effective way to control crime, whether through enforced disappearances or crossfire killings.
Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md Ali Hossain Fakir on Monday said police might resort to crossfire if the government allows it and it becomes necessary to maintain law and order and curb crimes.

item.title: Here is how you can save your electricity bill
item.description:
A refrigerator accounts for a large share of household electricity use, mainly because it runs 24 hours a day. Even minor mistakes in how it is used can noticeably inflate the monthly bill. According to experts, using the appliance properly can cut power consumption significantly.
Many people assume that only old refrigerators guzzle electricity. In reality, a few common mistakes can lead to wasted power in both new and old models. Regular maintenance and mindful use, those concerned say, are the most effective ways to save energy.
Experts stress that a refrigerator’s efficiency depends not only on the quality of the machine but also on the habits of the user. Following a few simple rules can lower your electricity bill and extend the life of the appliance.
Organize the interior When items are easy to find, the door does not have to stay open for long, so less cold air escapes.
Don’t keep the fridge completely empty A fridge with a moderate amount of food holds its temperature better than an entirely empty one.
Defrost regularly If your fridge does not have no-frost technology, excess ice can build up in the freezer and increase power consumption. The ice should be cleared at regular intervals.
Keep the vents clear Blocking the vents with food prevents cold air from circulating evenly, putting extra strain on the cooling system.
Keep the door shut during power cuts During load-shedding or an outage, keeping the door closed helps the fridge stay cold for much longer.
Allow air to circulate around the fridge Placing the fridge flush against a wall or furniture makes it harder for heat to escape, which can increase electricity use.
Choose the right size Using a refrigerator far larger than your family needs can result in unnecessary power consumption.
Experts say saving electricity requires mindful use of all household appliances, not just the fridge. But because a refrigerator never switches off, even small adjustments can add up to substantial savings in the long run.
They also suggest that if a refrigerator is very old or breaks down frequently, it may be worth considering a modern, energy-efficient model. With proper use and regular maintenance, households can lower their monthly bills while keeping their fridge in good working condition for years.

item.title: Do these five things every morning, and your memory may thank you at 80
item.description:
Mornings are rarely calm. Work deadlines, school runs, family duties and a dozen small chores leave little room for a quiet routine of one’s own.
Yet a 2025 survey by Nespresso and Project Healthy Minds found that nearly 90% of people believe the early moments of the day directly affect their mood and mental wellbeing for the rest of it.
Medical experts say the first few hours do more than lift the mood. They may also be key to protecting long-term brain health and keeping memory and thinking sharp into old age.
During sleep, the brain carries out a kind of overnight cleaning operation. Dr Eva L Feldman, a neurologist at the University of Michigan, explains that brain cells clear out waste while we sleep.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, this cleaning network is known as the glymphatic system, which uses fluid to flush harmful waste out of brain cells. The result is that the brain is at its freshest and sharpest soon after waking.
Dr Majid Fotuhi, a neuroscientist at the Brain Institute, says the first hour after waking sets the tone for the whole day. To keep the brain active and healthy over the long term, he recommends building five simple habits into the morning.
Taking on stress straight after waking is bad for the brain, says Dr Fotuhi. Prolonged stress releases the hormone cortisol, and high levels of it can damage cells in the hippocampus, the brain’s main center for learning and memory. Staying calm and optimistic in the morning therefore matters.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) suggests several ways to ease morning stress:
Rather than jumping up the moment the alarm rings, experts advise lying quietly for a few minutes and asking yourself a question.
Dr Fotuhi suggests: “How can I make today enjoyable?”
This is also a good moment to think about how to fit the five pillars of brain health into your day: exercise, a balanced diet, adequate sleep, stress management and intellectual stimulation. Doing so makes it easier to organize the day and keeps your mood buoyant.
Mental exercise early in the day stimulates the brain’s nerve cells, according to Dr Feldman. Reading, journaling, or solving puzzles such as sudoku and crosswords can sharpen the mind from the start of the day.
Dr Fotuhi also recommends writing down three intentions in a notebook each morning:
Morning exercise helps boost the performance of nerve cells, says Dr Feldman. Walking, running, cycling, swimming or yoga all improve blood flow to the brain. Exercise done in a group, through team sports or social activity, can also help preserve brain age.
A 2024 study published in the journal GeroScience found that 12 weeks of strength or resistance training produced structural changes in the hippocampus. These changes enhance neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to learn new things.
A breakfast rich in protein and fibre, with tea or coffee, is an excellent way to begin the day. Foods that are part of the mind diet in particular are well documented as helping to slow brain decline.
Adding leafy greens, nuts, olive oil, berries, chicken and fish to your morning meal supplies the brain with nutrients and helps preserve memory.
Dr Feldman stresses that it is never too late to start looking after the brain. Damage from smoking, drinking, or an irregular lifestyle becomes hard to reverse once symptoms appear.
The brain’s greatest strength, he notes, is neuroplasticity, meaning it can be rewired and strengthened at any age. These five small morning habits, practiced daily, could determine how sharp your memory and intellect remain in the years ahead.

item.title: Dr Yunus, other Asian humanitarians globally rank as ‘21st Century Merit Icons’
item.description:
Bangladesh's Nobel laureate and former chief adviser to the interim government Dr Muhammad Yunus has been indexed in a group of Asian notables recognized by the Britain-based merit-indexing body Impact Hallmarks (IH) as the 'Century Merit Icons'.
IH has named 38 individuals the 'The Merit Sovereigns of 21st Century', scored against a 1,000-point framework designed to reward documented achievement over public visibility.
Around eleven Asian icons appear in the top three of eight of the ten thematic categories, and fifteen more feature in the wider recognition tiers.
Nepal's Pushpa Basnet, China's Chen Si and Japan's Yukio Shige jointly secure 3rd place in 'Humanitarianism and Social Justice', while from Pakistan, late Bilquis Edhi tops the Legacy Memorial category and Arch-polymath Prof Aurangzeb Hafi secures a shared first place in 'Scientific Endeavours' category.
Unveiled in the Quarticentennial Merited Impacts Gazette (2000–2025), the list is billed as the first merit-based retrospective of the century's first quarter.
From an initial pool of 1.9 million notables across 195 countries, 150 independent assessors shortlisted 187 individuals using the Merited Impact Value (MIV) framework.
It weighs documentary evidence, systemic transformation and public resonance across four dimensions: Humanitarian Impact Merit (HIM), Scientific Impact Merit (SIM), Resilience Impact Merit (RIM) and Cumulative Impact Merit (CIM).
A global online poll served as a public validation layer.
Described by IH as the 'Arch-Polymath of 21st Century', Prof Aurangzeb Hafi is recognized in three categories.
In 'Scientific Endeavours', he shares first place with physicist Dr Fritjof Capra (US) on 950+ points.
He was cited for integrating the scientific pentarchy, identifying the alarming mega-toxification of underground water reserves caused by prevailing sewage-drainage practices in underdeveloped countries, for developing the 'Deca-Archic Phygital Literacy Model' and discovering the phenomenon of Magneto-Hydro-Tropism (MHT).
In Multiple Iconicities he is placed at second with 957 points for being a cross-disciplinary 'Arch-researcher', who integrates research across 93 epistemic subject-fields, behind James Harrison (Australia—965) and ahead of Nathan Myhrvold (US—945).
In Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons he placed third with 910 points, behind King Charles III (930) and physicist John Preskill (US—925).
Bilquis Edhi (Pakistan—965) leads the posthumous Legacy Memorial category for her Jhoola project, which provided shelter and medical care to abandoned infants.
Peter Higgs (UK—950) and Kofi Annan (Ghana—930) complete the top three. In Humanitarianism and Social Justice, three Asians share third place on 930+ points.
Yukio Shige (Japan), known as the 'Chotto Matte' ('wait a moment' man), leads volunteers credited with saving more than 750 people from suicide at the Tōjinbō cliffs.
Chen Si (China) also prevented hundreds of suicides. Pushpa Basnet (Nepal) founded organizations rescuing children who would otherwise grow up in prison with incarcerated parents.
In Scientific Endeavours, Fields Medalist Shing-Tung Yau (China) and H.E. Dr Mohamed Al-Kuwaiti (UAE) share second place on 920+ with Noam Chomsky and Dana Bolles (both US).
Cosmologist Prof. Chandra Wickramasinghe (Sri Lanka) is third on 910. Ghanim Al-Muftah (Qatar—939) places second in Luminary and Differently-Able Icons, behind Nick Vujicic (Australia/US—940).
Siti Atikoh Supriyanti (Indonesia—907), recognized for community-centred public health advocacy, features in Dignified Asceticism.
Bana Al-Abed (Syria—905), whose social media dispatches from besieged Aleppo drew international attention, is third among Young Trailblazing Icons.
The overall topper of the Gazette is Stephen Soldz (US—967), who leads Humanitarianism and Social Justice for documenting psychological coercion tactics used against war prisoners.
He was the first ethicist to make academic condemnation of employing the sacred religious texts as an instrument of torture.
Francesca Albanese (Italy) and Graça Machel (Mozambique) share second on 940+ points.
Albanese, United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, is recognized for her 2024 report "Anatomy of Genocide" and for facing sanctions over her work, while Machel is recognized for providing baselines for the UN's revolutionary research work on the effects of war on children.
Pope Francis (Vatican City—940) leads Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity, followed by Capra (935) and Greta Thunberg (Sweden-933).
Greta Thunberg is recognized for the arc running from her solitary school strike movement to leading the high-risk flotilla missions carrying aid toward Gaza including the Freedom Flotilla in June 2025 and the 44-nation Global Sumud Flotilla in September 2025, the interception of which led to 450 activists being detained, and sparked protests across three continents.
Tarja Halonen (Finland—920), Machel and Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand) lead Dignified Asceticism.
Usain Bolt (Jamaica—905), LeBron James (US—903) and Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal—902) top Athletics and Physical Excellence.
Orion Jean (US—935) and Greta Thunberg (920) head the Young Trailblazing Icons.
Pakistan's Dr Amjad Saqib, Sri Lanka's Jehan Perera, India's Arunima Sinha and the two young Pakistani siblings Fiddhah Hafiah and Ghulam Bishar Hafi are jointly heralded as the 'Five-pointed Asian Star'.
The results form part of the 'Sovereign Sesquicentennial Confluence of Intellect & Impact' (2026).
Full results would be archived in the Quarticentennial Merited Impacts Gazette, alongside the Quarticentennial Roll of Honour (HI©) to be published in due course.

item.title: Post-traumatic laughter in the age of self-censorship
item.description:
“Why does so little of Bangladesh’s contemporary art history survive anywhere except someone’s old Facebook album?” was one of the questions Sarridon Collective explored in their exhibition ‘triggered after s*x’, held at Daagi Art Garage from August 1–8,2026.
Months after it closed, those questions and the discussions around them still ruminate in my head.
The show looked not so much at tragedy as at the moments that come after, what Marx, extending Hegel, calls the tragedy that comes the second time as farce. The revolutionary moment dissolves, short-lived, and disillusionment follows right on the dopamine hit.
A bitter reminder to prepare for what’s to come.
Instead of relief there is greater tension; before we can process one tragedy, we are met with events of multiplied severity.
There is little possibility for a ‘post’-traumatic experience, because stress persists.
Looking at the hyperactive happenings of this ongoing melodrama, at tragedies dimmed by newer technologies of infrastructure and media, at our isolated strategies to mute our own weeping, feels, in retrospect, humorous.
Photo: Courtesy
I’d call this humor defiance or resistance, if those terms had not been used elsewhere to build the very thing the humor in this exhibit responds to.
In the post-politically correct era, where we have internalized the language of possible accusations and deniability, the jester’s joke stands elsewhere entirely.
It does not accuse or defend; it simply passes, reveals its truth, and acknowledges unspoken truths ostracised by, and outside of, old and emerging narratives.
It does not live in opposition, so it never loses its footing.
The exhibit, featuring artists Imran Firdaus, Shikdar Shaikat, Fahad Hossain Kazmee and Nafees Sabur, looks at national trauma through this joke, well aware of its own tendencies to self-censor and repress.
The trauma is now transnationalized. Shaikat’s illustrations reiterate the language of oppression through ridicule, lifting the veil on the close-knit habitus between neoliberalism and MAGA.
Kazmee’s paintings allude to the materiality of trauma through a missile piercing the vertebrae.
Sabur’s prose compositions on the mundane life of tragedy testify to structural violence in a subjectivity that changes its register as the political absurdities play out.
Firdaus’s video essay plays 13 film openings from 1972, in the newly formed nation, against the audio of the ongoing state radio, which somehow syncs on its own, offering the viewer a way to trace a pattern of origin and look at the self within.
The censored sex in the title, achieved through the asterisk, pulls the word out of the regular, otherwise mundane at best and medical at worst, and foreshadows the censorships the show wishes to talk about.
I visited twice and still couldn’t explore every artwork, , each visit a round trip of more than 30 km.
Between industrial buildings and tanneries in Hazaribag, a few minutes from the Buriganga, the show was inaugurated with a Constitution cake on an August afternoon, close to two years since the “mass uprising”.
What appealed to me immediately and lingered longest were Firdaus’s text cards, a cross between a guerrilla exhibition and a homage to love letters, written from the precipice of coming to terms with the precipice itself.
They are scattered on the floor like the ‘abashik hotel’ brothel adverts found on city footpaths and footbridges. The cards announce and confess poignant truths.
Their acceptance of our shared predicament echoes as the late-late-stage capitalist successor of chopping wood and carrying water; it is either the result of enlightenment or the path to it.
One card, in an omniscient voice, says “You are in tension because you lose attention”, which may suggest that tension comes from the body’s restlessness and inability to focus, in an economy where attention is currency, or it may point to an existential crisis of being unseen, the anxiety of evanescence.
“Ami tomar phone er bhetor ekbar ghure ashte chai” (I want to explore inside your phone once) replaces “mon” (the simple Bengali word for the unified spirit of the heart and mind, unconcerned with Cartesian dualism) with “phone” in a popular 2009 Bangla pop song.
Appropriately revised for a rapidly transforming era, where we still yearn for love (and suspect infidelity) even beneath a global technofascist, transhumanist project.
This doesn’t make the device an alternative to the heart.
It shows they are synonymous, and how we weave technologies into the emotional and the unconscious, producing newer forms of subjectivity.
It is not a mere moralistic critique of ‘consumption’, much as David Graeber rejects the reductive assumption that people are passive victims of products.
Firdaus’s wordplay is not a literal replacement of the real with the internet-mediated mechanical; it shows how technological artefacts hold the most human and visceral things: desire, insecurity, restlessness, longing. It also reminds me of his one-line poem, “Attyar shathe jantrik shomporko” (mechanical relationship with the soul), or, bent slightly, “jontrer shathe attik shomporko” (a soul relationship with the machine).
You find humor again in Shaikat’s digital collage “Porimoni Suffering From Severe Fever”, framed next to Firdaus’s vintage cinema clips.
The series tells of a plague that has captured the metropolis, in partly absurdist and partly Kafkaesque satire. Porimoni’s fever is treated like a state of emergency; chairs and table fans are “living”, going through the predicaments of the masses, grappling with depression and culture wars.
Some of the text will be familiar to the chronically online.
Photo: Courtesy
It is taken from real Facebook posts and comments, which stand alone as commentary on social realities, no longer bound to their creators.
One text, “the woman’s work is to stay at home and raise children”, appears with the wrong Bengali consonants, exactly as the original commenter posted it, which undeniably adds humor.
It reflects a tragic reality, but plays more as farce.
What catches the audience’s attention most is Shaikat’s book installation at the centre, laid on a table, wrapped in styrofoam and plastic like packaged meat, with photographs of raw beef and chicken on the cover.
This hyperreality brings unease, reminding us that nondegradable plastic almost immortalizes this period of our lives, full of inconvenient conveniences.
Who could have guessed the Kali Yuga would be so characterized by simulacra?
On the next wall, Kazmee paints the state of the corporeal in the Kali Yuga, the remains of ethnonationalist violence.
‘Anatomy of Hunger’ shows nameless skeletons, missiles, rubble and blood, and the multispecies scrambling in the ruins.
The fish, the bird, the crocodile have evolved into their deformation.
The monster in one painting has a nationalist icon for an eye. Kazmee’s thesis is quite straightforward. His hungry, consuming subject is far removed from those in the other artworks.
As Graeber reminds us, to consume means to use up, to “eat up, devour, waste, destroy, or spend”; and in Hegel’s view, we differ from other animals in desiring from lack.
The paradox in the master/slave dialectic relates to what Kazmee presents in his paintings of obliteration: what it means to really consume.
I had initially overlooked the series by the entrance, overwhelmed by the Bangla text that filled most of each composition, but revisiting it struck me.
Sabur’s series is, for lack of a better word, relatable to the citizens of this young and restless state.
His line on post-July iconoclasm and replacing the ‘fascist icon’ with new sculptures memorializing the movement related closely to my own work, which was fun to see; the fun is furthered by the text above a pixelated apple, “I enjoy being bitten but not all the time”.
Sabur’s prose plucks from the new political project, a gruesome news story that citizens have grown accustomed to and numb to.
Sabur’s series faces Shaikat’s on parallel walls.
They mirror each other, both satirizing the imperialist project, neoliberal ‘norms’ in bed with looming fundamentalism, and internet-induced culture wars, from a male subjectivity that suits the digital medium.
Mediums are tacit; they communicate before we can identify them.
Their work also shares a sense of the struggle and confusion that constructs and challenges masculinity. Shaikat’s choice to centre Porimoni, a widely ‘trolled’ yet desired public figure, connotes that impulse.
Perhaps it is most directly addressed by Sabur, in “us male tortoises”.
The male subjectivity is important, since it acts as the medium for the political theatre of the nation-state and urban life, which photographer Rahul Talukdar might call “Dhaka Opera”.
Men’s trauma, economic and sexual, goes unacknowledged, lacking language in legal and media discourse that refuses to even name it.
And since representation takes precedence in the drive for development and progress, perhaps what we need is a revised representation of men, and a revised understanding of themselves to themselves.
In “The Past That Never Told Me Its Name”, Firdaus’s five-minute stitch of the opening one to two minutes of 13 found films, out of the 29 released in newly independent Bangladesh in 1972, offers a space for introspection.
We see national trauma expressed through the local practice of melodrama, and the unavailability of the other 16 films raises the question of what survives and what was worth keeping as archive.
The audio comes from a radio set playing the state broadcast.
On the table beside the screen are copies of two legal documents: “The Censorship of Flims act,1963” and “The Cinematograph Act, 1918”. The clips are left as they are, “with no narrator telling you what to think”, as are the documents, but it still evokes a small grin.
“Political memory in Bangladesh does not only wound,” Firdaus writes in the concept note Satire and the Return of the Repressed , “it also produces absurdity, running jokes, the humour of a population that has learned to read between the lines of official language”.
The joke can only claim to be a joke, nothing more, and simultaneously a “confession dressed as comedy”.
I also think about the afterlife of the joke. But if archiving is what we do (or in some cases don’t do) with art, what about the joke?
When tools of resistance like art are co-opted, I think the same done to jokes fails far more miserably.
Appropriated humor becomes a sort of kitsch that does not quite trigger sincere, involuntary laughter and, at best, produces a simulation of it, a desire to be a part of it.
We see this in political cartoons, where genuine humor hardly gels with hypocrisy.
By the time such a cartoon is exploited as a centrepiece of a new narrative, the artist has already moved on to ridicule it, as the work of cartoonist Mehedi Haque may show.
Jokes reveal tacit truths, and their inherent refusal or inability to conform lets even the most self-censored subjects embody resistance beyond ideology.
“The exhibition,” Firdaus writes, “stands as the obscene, unserious cousin of testimony: no less political for being funny, no less true for arriving after the fact”.
Whether Sarridon Collective intended the show as a vehicle for somatic relief, satire, or both, its ability to sit with our own suffering and precarity is freeing.
This acceptance points towards the possibility of a spiritual life, giving a visual language to the complex, confusing predicaments we are still enduring.
The audience is allowed to touch the art, and its tactility, like the laughter the jokes may trigger, attempts to remind us of something about being human.
Maybe it is through suffering the profane that we can access the profound, not in spite of it. The show does not promise catharsis, but it can provoke a chuckle or laughter.
And that singular trigger might just be enough.
Ohama Raaz is a visual artist.

item.title: Desert flower
item.description:
O David, stop measuring the desert flowers
How long will the marigolds be measured by your fine veins?
The storm is whimpering for you, and a little rain
On a barren land yearning for you to return,
How long will the lilies be measured by your fine veins?
The Orange Globemallows are not burning in the sun, but in your fire.
Listen to the estranged Cactuses, David.
They carved your fine veins with warmth, water, and red.
Hardy, woody, and lovely they are!
How long will you protect them from your fine veins, David?
Suraya Akter prefers short poems; everything she writes is a draft except her poetry.

item.title: Faith has teeth
item.description:
I dyed my hair black last night.
This morning the sun came in like an accusation.
Yesterday I was blue and green,
all bruise and algae,
looking older than I am,
wiser than I wanted to be,
lost in the particular way
only the nearly-grown can be.
But this morning
I looked in the mirror
and she was gone.
Three months of blue,
three months of green,
three months of becoming someone
I could not recognise
were washed out by black.
My face looked younger.
Not beautiful.
Not happier.
Just younger.
Four years younger, almost.
I have not been fourteen in five years,
but there she was,
wearing my face again,
with the same foolish eyes,
the same mouth that had not yet learned
how often a promise can rot.
How strange
to look less lost
and feel more lost for it.
Yesterday I looked like someone
who had survived something.
Today I look like someone
who still believes she won't.
And isn't that the cruelest part?
At fourteen,
I had already decided my destiny.
I had named the roads,
picked the doors,
counted the years ahead of me
as though the future were a house
I could simply walk into.
I thought faith
was another word for knowing.
I did not know
faith could betray you.
I did not know
the girl who planned her life at fourteen
would grow up only to watch it
quietly become someone else's.
So here I am,
black-haired again,
four years older
and somehow four years younger,
standing in the morning light
looking like the girl I was
before the world taught me
that destiny is a liar
with a beautiful voice.
And God,
how young she looks.
How terrible
that she still looks like me.
Nubisha Rabya Topote, an XI-grade student at Holy Cross College, is a poet and writer
